articleTitle: Amid low detection, specialised stations to probe all cybercrimes in Karnataka
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Karnataka cybercrime detection rate
description: Although cybercrimes make up 32 per cent of total crimes in Karnataka, the detection rate is 18%.
body_raw: The Karnataka Police have decided that the 43 specialised cybercrime police stations, rather than jurisdictional police stations, will investigate all cybercrime cases in the state. This follows a high court order and a dispute within police ranks over the poor detection rate for cybercrimes in Karnataka, which ranks 30th in the country-a fact reportedly highlighted in a recent review by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to sources. Although cybercrimes make up 32 per cent of total crimes in Karnataka, the detection rate is 18 per cent, according to 2023 National Crime Records Bureau data, which places the state among the worst-performing ones for cybercrime detection. Jurisdictionallocal Police Stations shall continue to register complaints relating to Cyber Crime IT Act cases. However, after registration of FIR, the cases shall be immediately transferred to the concerned Cyber Crime Police Station in the District The concerned Cyber Crime Police Station shall immediately take up the case for investigation, says an order issued by the state police chief, Dr M A Saleem, on September 11. Cybercrime cases need timely preservation and analysis of digital evidence, technical examination of devices and electronic records, coordination with bankspayment intermediaries, telecom service providers, social media platforms and other agencies, besides prompt action for freezingholding suspected fraudulent transactions, it states. The supervision of cybercrime cases will vest with the superintendents of police in the districts and commissioners of police in cities, the order states. Cybercrimes have surpassed other crimes such as dacoity, robbery, and thefts in the state, where 52,000 cybercrime cases were reported in 2024, the highest in the country. Cyber Command Centre and court order The government created a Cyber Command Centre CCC last year under the leadership of a DGP-rank officer, Pranab Mohanty, to handle burgeoning cybercrime cases. The governments September 2, 2025 order said that cases under the Information Technology Act, the Aadhaar Act, and cases of fraud and cheating exceeding Rs 50 lakh must be mandatorily registered in cyber crime police stations. The Karnataka High Court later called for all cybercrime cases in the state to be handled by 43 cyber police stations. It also noted that jurisdictional police stations are overburdened with traditional policing work. The court then called for integrating the jurisdictional police stations with the CCC so that all cybercrimes would be brought under a single umbrella. If all of what is aforesaid is not complied with, in todays world, where crimes are faceless, investigations would become baseless, the court added. The number of cybercrimes reported in 2021 was 8,396 but grew to over 50,000 in 2025, the court pointed out. The graph has climbed steeply, a chilling reminder of the exponential growth of cybercrime. Thus, the CCC is not an option, but an imperative born of necessity, it stated. CCC responsible for cybercrime detection The new order also comes in the wake of a dispute over responsibility for the low cybercrime detection rate. The new order makes the CCC responsible for cybercrime detection. However, it is likely to cause hardship to victims of cybercrimes on account of the low count of cyber police stations in the state, a police source said.

articleTitle: A Dean’s dilemma in India’s AI Economy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: dean, ai
description: The problem is not that India has too many educated young people. It is that the relationship between qualification, competence and employment is becoming increasingly uncertain
body_raw: By Shama Rana A certain university dean recently told me, with some disappointment, that his daughter had decided to join an AI startup immediately after completing her undergraduate degree instead of pursuing a Masters to attain skills. His reaction was understandable. For generations of Indian academics and middle class families, education has followed a reassuring hierarchy. A Bachelors degree was good, a Masters was better, and a doctorate represented the highest form of intellectual accomplishment. More years spent studying generally meant better prospects and greater professional security. As someone currently navigating a doctoral programme myself, I found myself looking at the daughters decision differently. Perhaps she was not walking away from education at all. Perhaps she had simply recognised something our universities have been slower to acknowledge - in parts of the emerging economy, another degree is no longer automatically the most valuable next step. India has spent decades trying, rightly, to expand access to higher education. The Gross Enrolment Ratio for the 18 to 23 age group reached 29.5 in 2022-23, compared with 23.7 in 2014-15. That is an achievement. But expanding access raises another question what exactly are students gaining access to? The problem is not that India has too many educated young people. It is that the relationship between qualification, competence and employment is becoming increasingly uncertain. The Economic Survey 2024-25 offers a revealing picture. Among workers with graduate degrees, 38.23 per cent were in occupations requiring specialised skills, while 50.3 per cent were in semi-skilled occupations. Possessing a degree and finding work that actually uses the level of skill associated with it are not necessarily the same thing. Artificial intelligence makes this mismatch more urgent. Generative AI can already perform some routine cognitive work around which white-collar employment has traditionally been organised, from summarising documents and producing standard reports to elementary coding and procedural analysis. The Economic Survey 2025-26 acknowledges this shift and argues that education will increasingly need to cultivate reasoning, problem solving, communication and adaptability. Yet much of our educational culture continues to follow an older sequence accumulate knowledge, reproduce it in an examination, acquire the qualification and enter the labour market. AI unsettles that sequence because access to information is no longer scarce. The ability to reproduce information becomes less valuable when compared with the ability to interrogate it, connect it to a problem, recognise when it is wrong and use it intelligently. This does not make the university obsolete. The qualities universities can cultivate at their best, including critical thinking, disciplinary depth, intellectual curiosity and ethical reasoning, become more important when machines can generate plausible answers within seconds. Turning universities into coding academies would be a poor response to AI. But pretending disciplinary knowledge alone will be sufficient would be an equally serious mistake. An economics student should understand economic theory while knowing how contemporary tools can interrogate a dataset. A journalism student should understand reporting and ethics, but also how algorithms shape information and synthetic media complicates verification. A literature student need not become a programmer, but should understand how generative systems are changing authorship, publishing and intellectual property. These need not remain extracurricular skills acquired through separate online courses. India already has some architecture for this flexibility. The Academic Bank of Credits facilitates credit accumulation and transfer, while UGC provisions allow credits earned through platforms such as SWAYAM and NPTEL to be considered for accumulation and transfer. The principle is already established learning need not remain confined within a single classroom or rigid disciplinary pathway. Universities can now make that flexibility meaningful by allowing students to combine core disciplines with rigorously assessed modules responsive to technological and professional change. A mass communication student, for instance, could study media theory alongside data visualisation, computational research or AI-assisted verification. The aim is not to replace degrees with certificates, but to ensure that degrees remain connected to the world into which students graduate. The harder reform concerns institutional culture. Academic safeguards are necessary because curricula cannot be rewritten whenever a new technology becomes fashionable. But academic rigour cannot become an excuse for inertia. Departments need room to introduce electives, short modules and practitioner collaborations while preserving the intellectual foundations of their disciplines. There is also a cultural question. Indian families have long imagined educational progression as a ladder on which stopping can feel like falling behind. Bachelors, Masters, doctorate each additional qualification appears to promise greater security. Advanced study will remain indispensable for many professions, but it need not be the automatic next step for every graduate. The Economic Survey 2025-26 itself argues for a more fluid relationship between education and employment, including earn-and-learn pathways, recognition of short-form credentials and movement between education and work. This may prove particularly important when skills can change faster than conventional educational cycles. The Deans daughter may therefore represent something larger than one familys disagreement over a Masters degree. She belongs to a generation for whom education may cease to mean the uninterrupted accumulation of qualifications. A young person might graduate, work, return for specialised study, acquire another skill and later return to education again. India should not respond by diminishing the university or declaring the degree irrelevant. It should do something harder make the degree valuable enough that students seek higher education for what a university can uniquely give them, rather than because another qualification has become the price of entering the employment queue. In the AI economy, the question will no longer be simply how many degrees a young Indian possesses. It will be what, after acquiring them, she can actually understand, question and do. Rana is a Gurgaon-based writer and research scholar at MDU, Rohtak

articleTitle: Rakul Preet distances herself from Vashu Bhagnani I-T raids: ‘No Benami property’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rakul Preet Singh distances herself from IT raids. (Photo: Rakul Preet Singh/Instagram)
description: Rakul Preet Singh also urged publications and individuals who had carried what she described as “false, malicious and speculative reports” to retract them and clarify the facts.
body_raw: Nearly a week after the Income Tax Department conducted searches at several locations reportedly linked to Bollywood actor Rakul Preet Singh and her father-in-law, producer Vashu Bhagnani, the actress has issued a statement to set the record straight. Taking to her official Instagram handle, Rakul distanced herself from claims that she was involved in foreign remittances or held any benami properties. Have been paying taxes since the age of 20 The actress wrote, Its heartbreaking to see that theres a growing trend amongst the self styled online reporters some main stream media journalists to sensationalise the news without verifying facts. Lets therefore set the record straight once for all. In her statement, the actress claimed that the searches were not related to her, contrary to several reports that linked her to the investigation. Let it be known that I am from the Armed Forces background had no Godfather in the Industry. I have come up through sheer hardwork as a responsible law abiding citizen have been paying my due taxes since the age of 20 years, she wrote. Not involved in any foreign remittances on behalf of any production house Rakul further clarified that she is not involved in any foreign remittances, either in her personal capacity or on behalf of any production house. However, she did not specifically mention Pooja Entertainment, the production company associated with her father-in-law. The actor also denied holding any benami properties on behalf of anyone in India or abroad. I would also add here that I do not hold any Benami property on behalf of anyone anywhere in the country or abroad. Neither ANYONE has EVER gifted me any property at anytime nor do I accept such expensive gifts as a principle, she added. ALSO READ Ajay Devgns Drishyam 3 writer says wrote 100 versions of film Friends tried to bribe me for ending Rakul also urged publications and individuals who had carried what she described as false, malicious and speculative reports to retract them and clarify the facts. I understand that everyone running a media business however big has their own commercial pressures. But it cannot come at the cost of facts. And certainly not at the cost of someones reputation and livelihood, she said. What prompted Rakul Preet Singh to put out this statement? On September 28, the Mumbai Income Tax Department reportedly conducted searches at 12 locations over suspected financial irregularities. According to reports, investigators suspect that funds may have been routed abroad under the guise of financing film projects. Soon after reports of the Income Tax searches surfaced online, it was also reported that Vashu Bhagnani had been hospitalised in London. However, the reason for his hospitalisation has not been disclosed. According to NDTV, when the publication reached out to the Bhagnani family for a statement, they requested the media to leave them alone. While Rakul has distanced herself from the controversy, she has not mentioned her father-in-law or Pooja Entertainment by name in her statement. Her husband and actor-producer Jackky Bhagnani, meanwhile, has also remained silent amid the controversy. On the work front, the actress is gearing up for the release of Ramayana, in which she will play the role of Shurpanakha.

articleTitle: 3 women, 3 hotel rooms, 3 murders, and 1 police warning about couples
articleFeaturedImageAlt: On Friday, police broke open the door of a room in a small hotel in Miyapur and made a grisly discovery: the decomposing body of a 27-year-old medical student.
description: Police ask hotels to be on alert about couples checking in, but only one partner leaving
body_raw: The murder of three young women in separate incidents in hotel rooms over the past 10 days in Hyderabad has put the police on edge and the spotlight on small hotels renting out rooms for cheap. Police are now asking hotels and lodges to be alert, especially if a couple hires a room and one of them leaves and does not return. A particular focus is on customers using fake IDs to book rooms. Police on Monday warned hotels that if they do not verify whether Aadhaar or other IDs are authentic, they will face legal action. The Telangana Hotels Association has also urged hotels to exercise caution and thoroughly verify documents. Murder 1 On Friday, police broke open the door of a room in a small hotel in Miyapur and made a grisly discovery the decomposing body of a 27-year-old medical student. According to the police, the woman became acquainted with a man named Ravi Kumar on social media, and they entered into a relationship. Ravi borrowed heavily from her, including a gold chain, citing family emergencies but promising to return everything soon. When she pressed him, he asked her to come to Hyderabad, where he would return the jewellery. They checked into the hotel on September 30, and at some point Ravi left alone. Police said that when the womans father called her, her phone was switched off. When she did not return to the hostel on Saturday, her friends also alerted her father, who then lodged a police complaint. Cops traced her last mobile phone location to the hotel, where they discovered her decomposing body. Police say she was smothered with a pillow and Ravi is absconding. Murder 2 On September 29, a 34-year-old bank customer care executive was found dead inside a hotel room in SR Nagar. The woman had checked into the hotel with her partner, A Srinivas, who used a fake identity card. Both of them hail from Vikarabad but work and live in Hyderabad, police said. When Srinivas was leaving the hotel alone with his bag on Tuesday at 330 am, a staff member did ask him if the woman was also leaving, but he claimed that she would check out in the morning after having breakfast, the police said. It was not until late afternoon that the staff called police, after she did not answer the door for several hours. Deputy Commissioner of Police DCP A Ramana Reddy said that the woman was hit on the head with a blunt instrument, probably a curtain rod, causing her death. They may have had a quarrel late in the night, and he allegedly attacked her while she was eating. There were multiple injuries on her body. A plate of unfinished meal was found beside her on the bed, an official said. Police found that the accused does odd jobs in the Telugu film industry and is currently on the run. Teams have been sent to search in his native village. Murder 3 On September 22, a 29-year-old woman was taken to a hospital at Kothaguda by her male friend, with whom she was staying at a nearby hotel. Police said that the woman, who hailed from Jharkhand, and her friend, S Ravi Teja, who hails from Anakapalli in Andhra Pradesh, were working in the hospitality sector and had checked in a day earlier. On the morning of September 22, Ravi told hotel staff that the woman was unconscious, and they rushed her to a hospital, where she was declared dead on arrival. Ravi allegedly fled the spot, police said. Officials of Madhapur Police Station said there were injuries on the back of her head and face. Police traced the man to Visakhapatnam, where he attempted suicide and was admitted to King George Hospital. He was arrested on his release and brought to Hyderabad. According to the police, he confessed that he hit her with a blunt object as she was pressuring him to marry her. He was in an inebriated condition when he allegedly assaulted her, police said, and later fell asleep and woke up to find her dead.

articleTitle: Nobel prize for medicine: How it can help with Parkinson’s, epilepsy and memory
articleFeaturedImageAlt: nobel prize in medicine 2026
description: The technology can function as both a research tool and a roadmap for developing future therapies like Parkinson’s and depression.
body_raw: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for their ground-breaking discovery of channelrhodopsin algae protein and the development of optogenetics, a revolutionary technique that uses light to precisely control living neurons. This pioneering work, which successfully bridges biology and engineering to map complex neural circuits, earned the laureates a shared prize of 12 million Swedish kronor approximately 1.2 million USD. In simple terms, they found a way to control cells with light. Imagine that the brain is a vast electrical network containing billions of tiny cells called neurons. These neurons communicate by sending electrical signals, allowing us to move, see, remember, feel pain and experience emotions. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel helped scientists develop a remarkable way of controlling these electrical signals using light. Their research led to the discovery and development of light-sensitive proteins, called opsins, that can be placed in specific cells. When light is shone on those cells, the proteins act like tiny switches, turning the cells activity on or off. This technology is known as optogenetics - essentially, using light to control genetically modified cells. BREAKING NEWS The 2026 NobelPrize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. - The Nobel Prize NobelPrize October 5, 2026 Why is that such a big deal? Until optogenetics, scientists had relatively crude ways of figuring out what individual groups of neurons actually do. For example, electrical stimulation might activate many neighbouring neurons at once, making it difficult to know which cells were responsible for an effect. Researchers can now change that. They can make a particular group of neurons light-sensitive and then activate or silence those cells with extraordinary precision. It is a little like moving from switching off the electricity to an entire building to being able to control one particular light bulb. Whats the most important application so far? Scientists can use optogenetics to ask questions that were previously extremely difficult to answer Which neurons cause a seizure? Which brain circuits are involved in addiction? Which cells are responsible for forming a memory? Which circuits contribute to depression or chronic pain? By switching particular cells on and off and observing what happens, researchers can establish much stronger cause-and-effect relationships between brain activity and behaviour. Could it lead to treatments for brain diseases? This is where the research could have a major medical impact. Diseases such as Parkinsons disease, epilepsy, depression and chronic pain involve abnormal activity in particular neural circuits. If scientists can identify exactly which cells or circuits are malfunctioning, they may eventually be able to target those circuits much more precisely than conventional treatments can. So the technology can function as both a research tool and a roadmap for developing future therapies. Can it restore sight? Optogenetics has also opened a completely new approach to treating certain forms of blindness. In some inherited retinal diseases, the photoreceptor cells that normally detect light are destroyed. Researchers have explored introducing light-sensitive proteins into other surviving retinal cells, effectively giving those cells a new ability to respond to light.Human studies have provided early proof that this approach can produce some visual perception in people with severe retinal degeneration. It is not yet a general cure for blindness but demonstrates how scientists can potentially use the principles of optogenetics to build a new light-detection system inside a damaged nervous system. The technology may extend beyond the brain Researchers are investigating light-controlled biological systems involving immune cells, cellular signalling and drug delivery. In the longer term, such approaches could potentially allow medicines or biological processes to be switched on only at a particular location or at a particular time.That could be particularly valuable in medicine, where one of the biggest challenges is often doing something to the diseased cells without affecting healthy cells. The significance of Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagels work goes beyond a single treatment or device.They helped give scientists something that biology had largely lacked a precise control switch for individual cells. Instead of simply watching neurons fire, researchers can manipulate them and ask what happens. The immediate payoff has been a revolution in basic neuroscience the longer-term promise is a new generation of highly targeted treatments for disorders of the brain, nervous system and potentially other organs.

articleTitle: Video shows SHO pulling gun during Bihar flood relief, suspended
articleFeaturedImageAlt: An aerial view of the flood-affected area following the rise in the Ganga River water level. (ANI Photo)
description: The video comes days after a man died during an aerial drop of relief material in Saran, where flooding has affected over 3 lakh people and disrupted road access to several areas.
body_raw: Days after a man died during an airdrop of flood relief material from a helicopter in Saran, another video from the district shows the station house officer SHO of Maker allegedly displaying his service pistol during the distribution of relief material. The officer, Sangram Kumar Singh, has been suspended with immediate effect, with the police ordering an inquiry into the purported circumstances captured in the video. The video circulating on social media shows Singh standing on top of one of two pickup vehicles as people appear to queue up in front of the vehicle. At one point, when a person appears to try to pull a bag out of the pickup, the SHO is seen jumping onto the vehicle, warning people to stay back, then briefly pulling out his pistol and pointing it at the group. In an order issued on October 4, the Saran Senior Superintendent of Police cited the video and said it prima facie reflected gross negligence, indiscipline and arbitrariness in the discharge of his duties, suspending Singh with immediate effect. He will be attached to the Saran Police Centre during suspension, the order said. A separate statement from the SSPs office said it had found prima facie negligence and indiscipline and that it was investigating the alleged incident. The incident comes amid intensified relief operations in flood-hit Saran. The ration packets are currently being air-dropped. According to sources, the helicopter was arranged from Gorakhpur because flooding and waterlogging had made road access to some areas difficult. On October 2, Anil Kumar Singh, also known as Appu Singh, died in Parshurampur during the air-drop operation, while another person was injured. Police had said the cause of death would be established through a post-mortem examination, claiming there were no external injury marks on the body and that residents accounts of how he died differed. Flooding has affected large parts of Saran, with relief and rescue operations underway across the district. The administration had reported 170 affected villages in 33 panchayats across seven blocks, with over 3 lakh people affected. By October 3, Indian Air Force helicopters had made 15 sorties, dropping more than 5,600 dry-ration packets containing over 28 tonnes of food material, officials claimed.

articleTitle: Father from Botswana, mother from India: 5 cheetah cubs at Kuno usher in new lineage
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Five cheetah cubs born at Kuno National Park to a Botswana-born father and India-born mother (Image: @byadavbjp/X)
description: The births take India’s cheetah population to 60, of which 41 have been born in the country. The development comes just months after India brought a fresh group of cheetahs from Botswana to strengthen the genetic base of Project Cheetah
body_raw: An Indian-born cheetah has given birth to five cubs at Kuno National Park after mating with a Botswana Cheetah - ushering in the Botswana lineage of Indias cheetah population. KJP21, a 32-month-old female born in India, gave birth to the five cubs on Monday. Their father is a male cheetah brought from Botswana, making the newborns the first representatives of the Botswana lineage to be born in India, Union Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Bhupender Yadav said. The births take Indias cheetah population to 60, of which 41 have been born in the country. KJP21 is the third female cheetah born in India to reproduce, after Mukhi and KGP12. With the arrival of these five cubs, the cheetah population in India has reached 60, including 41 Indian-born cheetahs. Importantly, these cubs also mark the beginning of the Botswana lineage in India, as their father is a Botswana male cheetah - adding a new genetic lineage to Indias growing cheetah population, Union Minister Yadav said. Another historic and joyous milestone for Project Cheetah KJP21, a 32-month-old Indian-born female cheetah, has given birth to five healthy cubs in Kuno National Park today. KJP21 is the third Indian-born female cheetah to give birth, after Mukhi and KGP12-an important milestone in the emergence of the next generation of Indias cheetah population. With the arrival of these five cubs, the cheetah population in India has reached 60, including 41 Indian-born cheetahs. Importantly, these cubs also mark the beginning of the Botswanan lineage in India, as their father is a Botswanan male cheetah-adding a new genetic lineage to Indias growing cheetah population. Another generation born on Indian soil, adding yet another beautiful chapter to the remarkable story of cheetah reintroduction in India. Heartfelt congratulations to the veterinarians, field staff, managers and everyone associated with Project Cheetah, whose dedication, commitment and tireless efforts have made these moments possible. Welcome to the world, little ones WildlifeWeek2026 - Bhupender Yadav byadavbjp October 5, 2026 Boost to Project Cheetah The development comes just months after India brought a fresh group of cheetahs from Botswana to strengthen the genetic base of Project Cheetah. Nine cheetahs - six females and three males - arrived at Kuno from Botswana in February this year. They were the third group of cheetahs brought to India, after eight from Namibia in 2022 and 12 from South Africa in 2023. The decision to bring cheetahs from Botswana followed a fresh round of government-to-government discussions that began in December 2024. The Union government formally approached Botswana as it looked to expand the genetic base of Project Cheetah beyond the animals already brought from Namibia and South Africa. Environment Minister Yadav took up the proposal with Botswanas then Environment and Tourism Minister Boipuso Wynter Mmolotsi. Botswana agreed to partner with India after considering the countrys detailed Action Plan for Cheetah Reintroduction. The partnership received a political push during President Droupadi Murmus state visit to Botswana in November 2025. During her visit, Murmu and Botswana President Duma Gideon Boko witnessed the symbolic release of eight cheetahs, captured from the Ghanzi region, into a quarantine facility at the Mokolodi Nature Reserve. The choice of Botswana was significant because the country has one of Africas largest remaining wild cheetah populations. The first batch from Botswana was transported from the Mokolodi Nature Reserve to Gaborone and then flown to India with the assistance of the Indian Air Force before being taken by helicopter to Kuno. After the November handover, the animals underwent quarantine and the two sides worked through the necessary permissions, including export and CITES clearances, veterinary requirements and arrangements for transporting the animals to India. A three-member Botswana delegation, including veterinarians and an anti-poaching expert, subsequently visited both Kuno National Park and Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary and held discussions with National Tiger Conservation Authority officials in Delhi.

articleTitle: Arijit Singh announces first India tour since retirement, to perform in nine cities
articleFeaturedImageAlt: arijit singh update
description: Arijit Singh's last India tour was One Night Only – India Tour, which concluded in Delhi in March 2023.
body_raw: Arijit Singh has announced a nine-city India tour, which will kick off in January 2027 and conclude in May the same year. The playback singer will travel to Ahmedabad, Chandigarh, Jaipur, Mumbai, Bengaluru, New Delhi, Pune, Indore and Hyderabad as part of a tour celebrating his two-decade-long musical journey. The upcoming tour marks Arijits first major India tour since he announced his decision to stop taking on new playback singing assignments earlier this year. Talking about the tour, Arijit said in a statement, 20 years of music is a journey I feel very grateful for. The greatest part of it has always been the people, the listeners who have given these songs a life of their own. He added, I am really looking forward to travelling across India and experiencing that love together, live on stage. There are so many songs, so many memories and so many people to meet. I cant wait. According to reports, the concert experience will feature 360-degree spatial audio, kinetic LED fixtures, panoramic screens, laser arrays and stadium-scale pyrotechnics. The live production is being designed to create an immersive experience for fans. ALSO READ Rakul Preet distances herself from Vashu Bhagnani I-T raids No Benami property The tour is presented by Kotal Solitaire and produced and promoted by Team Innovation. Mohit Bijlani, Founder of Team Innovation, said in a statement, Every single detail of this journey is being designed to world-class standards, offering fans a live experience at a scale never seen before in his home country. Arijit Singhs last India tour was One Night Only-India Tour, which concluded in Delhi in March 2023. The tour covered Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Bengaluru and Delhi. Previously, announcing his retirement, Arijit Singh wrote on Instagram, Hello. Happy New Year to all. I want to thank you all for giving me so much love all these years as listeners. I am happy to announce that I am not going to take any new assignments as a playback vocalist from now on. I am calling it quits. It was a wonderful journey. Despite his announcement, several of Arijits songs have continued to feature in films as part of prior commitments. These include Phir Se from Dhurandhar The Revenge, Ghar Kab Aaoge from Border 2, all five songs from the Junaid Khan-starrer Ek Din, and Tujhko from Cocktail 2. He has also lent his voice to Salman Khans Matrubhoomi.

articleTitle: Shreyas Iyer looks to go higher and higher after Asian Games gold
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Shreyas Iyer led India to 2026 Asian Games gold medal. (CREIMAS)
description: After a difficult start, Shreyas Iyer has started to find his feet as India’s T20I captain, especially in how he uses his bowlers and backs young players. The West Indies series will be his next test.
body_raw: By the time Shreyas Iyer turned to Shivam Dube in the fifth and final T20I against England in Southampton, there was little left to salvage. England were 2251, with Jos Buttler and Harry Brook in control. Dube didnt bowl until the 19th over. He took two wickets, but gave away 22 runs. It was a snapshot of where Iyer was he had the resources, but was still figuring out how to use them. England ended with 2573, and India lost by 56 runs. The defeat completed a 0-4 series loss and was Iyers sixth defeat in seven matches as Indias T20I captain. Southampton felt like the nadir of a difficult start. There was little then to suggest things would turn for the better. Yet they have. Over the next nine matches, all of them wins, Iyer may not have become a master tactician. But there seems to be a clearer identity about his captaincy, especially how he uses his bowlers. The Ireland and England matches hinted at a captain still trying to work out which bowler fitted where. The games since have shown greater role clarity, more trust in young players and, crucially, a willingness to back them after things go wrong. The change is perhaps best seen in how Iyer handles young pacers when things dont go to plan. Mayank Yadav, after taking a first-ball wicket in the third T20I, was hit for a six in his next spell. Iyer still brought him back to break the fifth-wicket partnership between Wessly Madhevere and Ryan Burl and then trusted him with the 20th over. Mayank showed enough in Zimbabwe to suggest that he could become an important cog in the attack. But there is still work to do. His pace is his biggest asset, but the next step is to trust his plans when batsmen attack him, rather than relying on pace to get out of trouble. ALSO READ Jadejas relevance has faded, and he is no longer Indias Mr Utility Prince Yadavs role seems clear bowl hard lengths to top-order batsmen and keep going even if the ball disappears. He struck with his first ball in the second T20I against Zimbabwe and then removed Sikandar Raza in the same spell, both wickets coming from that approach. After the first game, Prince said the message from Iyer and the coaches was simple - keep bowling the right lengths and dont worry if a good ball gets hit. With Hardik Pandya still unavailable, India are developing Nitish Kumar Reddy in the seam bowling all-rounder role. Against Afghanistan in the third T20I, he conceded 15 in his first over. Iyer did not shelve him. He brought him back in the ninth and then again in the 11th and 13th over. Nitish finished with 325 in his four overs. Abhishek Sharma perhaps best captures what Iyer is trying to build. In the first T20I against Afghanistan in Delhi, Iyer gave Abhishek an over despite having regular bowling options and that experimentation continued at the Asian Games, despite the main bowlers having overs left. India have often played with only five frontline bowlers, and Iyer looks keen to develop a sixth bowling resource. Sanjay Manjrekar, who has watched Iyer over the years for India and in the IPL, believed Iyer looked more settled in the role now after the early stutter. One thing, whatever little you can get, you know, the vibe, just being around him - did a couple of tosses with him and just being there - he seems like hes settled into the role. Suddenly it seems like he has grown, you know, maturity and everything. So he must have realised after the Ireland experience that you just do your best and the results are beyond your control, he said. Despite the nine wins, however, Iyers captaincy is still developing. It is too early to call him a finished product. Bigger tests lie ahead, starting with the West Indies series in Lucknow on Tuesday. Manjrekar does not see the coming challenge as simply a test of Iyer. I think the test for this Indian T20 team will be performing in different conditions. That makes the West Indies series important. India have played just one series at home under his captaincy, with all three matches in Delhi. Against West Indies, across five venues and different conditions, we will see how he adapts his methods and whether the identity he is developing is long-lasting. The early defeats showed a captain looking for the right combinations and ways to use his bowlers. Since then, he has looked more comfortable giving players responsibility and allowing them to grow into their roles. There will be missteps, and some risks will not pay off. But that is part of the process. More importantly, Iyer no longer looks to be searching for an identity. He looks to be building one. India vs West Indies, first T20I, Live on Star Sports Network and JioHotstar, 7 pm.

articleTitle: ‘Must run to the bed’: Amitabh Bachchan opens up on sleep struggles ahead of 84th birthday
articleFeaturedImageAlt: amitabh bachchan on KBC 18
description: Acknowledging the importance of sleep, Amitabh Bachchan said he now wants to make an effort to go to bed early so that he can rest and be ready to wake up early for work.
body_raw: Just a week before turning 84, Amitabh Bachchan has revealed that he struggles to find time to sleep. With a packed work schedule and an extremely active mind, the veteran actor said it can be difficult for him to get enough rest. Taking to his blog, the actor wrote, They said the night sleep is the best repair mechanism of the human body. and I struggle to find the time to follow that. Acknowledging the importance of sleep, Amitabh Bachchan said he now wants to make an effort to go to bed early so that he can rest and be ready to wake up early for work. Sharing what keeps him from sleeping, the actor wrote, It is a different feel. a state of many thoughts and ideas. all filled with drive and a sense of conquering all that was once considered as a goal. He added that this excitement to achieve more gives him the power to keep moving towards his goals and reach his destination in time. He concluded, And I must run to the bed. Last week, Amitabh Bachchan revealed on the sets of Kaun Banega Crorepati that he had slipped and injured his knee during a shoot. ALSO READ Yami Gautam-Aditya Dhar not moving to Himachal Pradesh, filmmakers team clarifies After making his grand entry on the show, Amitabh quickly chose to sit down. Explaining the reason, he said, Usually, I do my monologue standing at the centre, but today, I have a knee injury. Yesterday, during the shoot, I slipped and fell and injured my knee. The veteran star pointed towards his left knee while talking about the injury. After noticing the audiences worried expressions, he was quick to clarify that the injury was not serious. He explained that he chose to sit because he was having a little bit of difficulty standing up. Soon after the incident, however, Amitabh was seen attending a book launch event in Mumbai alongside his wife and actor Jaya Bachchan and legendary writer Gulzar. Even at 84, Amitabh Bachchan continues to remain active in the entertainment industry. From hosting the popular quiz show Kaun Banega Crorepati on Sony to appearing in films such as Vettaiyan and Uunchai, the actor continues to take on new projects. In 2024, he played the role of Ashwatthama in Nag Ashwins Kalki 2898 AD, performing several action sequences in the film. He is set to reprise the role in the second instalment of the franchise.

articleTitle: Blue economy: How to make maritime expansion a lasting source of prosperity
articleFeaturedImageAlt: India, blue economy, finance
description: While India seeks to harness its vast maritime wealth, it remains committed to making the blue economy inclusive and sustainable. How can it effectively connect economic growth, finance, livelihoods, and conservation? And how can it attract the long-term capital needed to support the sector’s expansion? See infographics.
body_raw: - Pushpendra Singh and Archana Singh What might a richer coastline look like? It could mean more ports, bigger ships, and higher seafood exports. It could also mean higher income for fishing families, clean waters, and better protection for coastal villages from storms. An integrated approach that balances these objectives will be crucial to making Indias Blue Economy inclusive and sustainable. As the Blue Revolution is set to be another success story, lets understand how India seeks to harness its marine wealth. Ocean as the engine of growth For decades, Indias infrastructure story was written largely on land. Roads connected markets, railways moved freight, and industrial corridors attracted investment. The sea entered this story mainly through ports and trade. Now, India is looking at the ocean as a wider economic space for fisheries, tourism, energy, research, and new industries. Indias blue economy ambitions are complemented by its 11,098 km of coastline. The blue economy refers to the sustainable use of ocean and coastal resources to support economic growth, jobs and livelihoods, while protecting marine ecosystems. Its scope extends beyond fishing and shipping to emerging fields like marine biotechnology and ocean energy. Indias maritime activity is already growing. The countrys major ports handled 915.17 million tonnes MT of cargo during FY 202526, marking a year-on-year growth of 7.06. This underscores the growing efficiency of Indias maritime sector. Building Indias blue economy Alongside its extensive coastline, Indias maritime infrastructure supports around 95 of the countrys trade by volume. As the government aims to increase the maritime sectors contribution to GDP significantly by expanding maritime infrastructure, Sagarmala has played a crucial role in this. The ambitious port-led infrastructure development programme, launched in 2015, has supported port-led development through various initiatives. Around 845 projects, estimated at Rs 6.06 lakh crore, have been taken up under the Sagarmala programme, according to an assessment by the government. As of March 24, 2026, around 315 projects worth Rs 1.57 lakh crore have been completed, while 210 projects are currently under implementation, and 320 projects are in the planning stage. Better links between waterways, ports, roads and railways can improve freight movement, reduce transport costs and strengthen the competitiveness of Indian businesses. But the blue economy is not merely about transport. It also encompasses food security, energy, livelihoods and the scientific knowledge needed to manage ocean resources sustainably. Fisheries, economy, and livelihoods Fisheries show how closely economic opportunity is linked with everyday life. The sector supports nearly 30 million livelihoods through inland fisheries and aquaculture, not just marine fishing. This distinction matters when discussing coastal development. The fisheries sector has evolved into a commercially significant sector over the past decade. India is now the second largest fish-producing country and accounts for about 8 of global fish production. Its seafood exports span a wide and diversified basket, with over 350 varieties of products shipped to nearly 130 global markets. Seafood export earnings registered a strong growth, rising from Rs 62,408 crore in 2024-25 to Rs 73,890 crore in FY 2025-26 an increase of about 18.4. While the growth underscores the sectors economic potential, translating this into returns for producers and workers remains important. For fishing families, this requires safe landing facilities, ice plants, cold storage, affordable credit and access to markets. Better processing can reduce losses and raise earnings without putting additional pressure on fish stocks. Cooperatives can improve bargaining power, while women in processing and marketing may also need stronger support. Investing in new ocean opportunities Further offshore, India is exploring new possibilities. A 7,453-crore government scheme supports the development of one gigawatt of offshore wind capacity - 500 MW each off the coast of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu - along with port upgrades. These are planned investments, rather than operating capacity. The 4,077-crore Deep Ocean Mission covers underwater technologies, biodiversity, ocean observation and deep-sea exploration. The research into seabed resources may widen future opportunities, but exploration does not establish that commercial extraction is ready or environmentally sound. However, these activities show why maritime development needs different kinds of finance. Ports require large investments with long repayment periods. Fishing enterprises need smaller loans and insurance. The research and conservation often require public funding, as their benefits far outweigh commercial returns. Blue bonds and the maritime financing gap How can India bring long-term capital into this expanding economy? Blue bonds offer a route. A blue bond is a borrowing instrument whose proceeds are reserved for sustainable water and ocean-related projects. Like a conventional bond, it must be repaid with interest. Its distinguishing feature is the specified use of funds and environmental reporting. Market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India SEBI recognises the potential of blue bonds for the countrys blue economy. Its 2023 framework introduced blue bonds within debt securities. Their scope includes clean water, recycling, sustainable shipping and fishing, traceable seafood, ocean energy and ocean mapping. However, a projects location beside the sea does not automatically make it eligible for blue financing. For maritime infrastructure, long-term bonds can help match borrowing periods with the years projects need to generate income. They can also attract institutional investors seeking long-duration investment opportunities. But a blue bond remains a debt instrument and needs a credible repayment plan. Indias first proposed blue bond, under the Sagarmala programme, offers a case in point. Sagarmala Finance Corporation planned to raise Rs 600 crores through 10-year bonds but withdrew the issue on September 28 after investors sought higher interest rates than it was willing to offer. Bids totaled 525 crores. However, the setback does not remove the case for blue finance. It shows that a sustainability label alone cannot guarantee lower borrowing costs. Affordable borrowing requires sound projects, reliable income and a financial structure that addresses risk. Environmental objectives, therefore, need to be backed by financial credibility. What global experiences show Other countries offer useful lessons. Seychelles issued the worlds first sovereign blue bond in 2018, raising USD 15 million. A USD 5 million World Bank guarantee and USD 5 million in concessional financing from the Global Environment Facility helped support the transaction. However, Belize followed a different approach. Its USD 364 million debt conversion in 2021 refinanced sovereign debt while creating funding for marine conservation and supporting a commitment to protect 30 per cent of its ocean. This was a debt-for-conservation arrangement, rather than simply a bond financing new infrastructure. Indias scale and financing needs are different, but these examples offer useful insights blue finance works better when financial support is clearly linked to environmental results. Guarantees or concessional funding should serve measurable public benefits, with their costs disclosed. Growth without bluewashing Finance alone cannot make maritime growth sustainable. A port can increase trade while damaging mangroves. Tourism can create jobs while adding waste. Bigger fishing fleets can raise catches in the short-term but can reduce stocks over time. India needs clear standards to prevent bluewashing - attaching a blue label to projects without convincing environmental benefits. Independent review, transparent use of funds, and regular reporting can help establish what investments have achieved. This could include measures such as reductions in pollution, protection of marine habitats, and improvements in the livelihoods of coastal communities. Indias blue economy will, therefore, need to effectively connect growth, finance, livelihoods, and conservation from the outset. Coastal communities need a meaningful voice. The goal is to make the ocean more productive without undermining the ecosystems. That balance will determine whether maritime expansion becomes a lasting source of prosperity. Post read questions 1. Indias Blue Economy represents a shift from a port-centric maritime strategy towards a broader economic engagement with ocean resources. Discuss the opportunities and challenges associated with this transition. 2. The success of Indias Blue Economy will depend not merely on expanding maritime infrastructure, but on balancing economic growth with ecological sustainability and coastal livelihoods. Discuss. 3. Fisheries illustrate the dual character of Indias Blue Economy-as a source of economic growth and as a foundation for millions of livelihoods. Discuss the measures required to make fisheries growth more inclusive and sustainable. 4. Sagarmala reflects Indias attempt to leverage its coastline for port-led development. Assess its potential to reduce logistics costs and improve competitiveness while examining the limitations of a predominantly infrastructure-led approach to the Blue Economy. 5. What are blue bonds? How can they help finance Indias maritime and ocean-related development? Discuss the challenges involved in making blue finance both affordable and environmentally credible. Pushpendra Singh is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Somaiya Vidyavihar University, Mumbai, and Archana Singh is an Assistant Professor of Gender and Economics at the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai.
