description: Proposal discussed at meeting involving district administration, police and other stakeholders, including temple committee and taxi union, Express has learnt
body_raw: The Nainital district administration is set to introduce a registration system for pilgrims visiting Kainchi Dham, initially on weekends, as the Kumaon shrine grapples with a sharp rise in visitors and traffic congestion, The Indian Express has learnt. The proposed system will be modelled on the registration mechanism used for Uttarakhands Char Dham pilgrimage and is expected to allow the administration to know in advance how many devotees are expected at the shrine on a given day and regulate the flow when crowds swell. Currently, there is no registration requirement to visit Kainchi Dham. Pilgrims can arrive at the shrine and enter for darshan without any prior registration. Nainital District Magistrate Lalit Mohan Rayal told The Indian Express Wednesday that a joint report by him and the Senior Superintendent of Police will be sent to the state governments Tourism Department recommending the system. The proposal is to introduce registration at Kainchi Dham, similar to what is done for Char Dham, Rayal told The Indian Express. A joint report of the DM and SSP will be sent to the government. The proposal was discussed at a meeting involving the district administration, police and other stakeholders, including the temple committee and taxi union on Tuesday. For now, the administration plans to restrict the system to weekends, when the shrine sees its largest crowds. We will keep it for weekends, Rayal said. Later, when the regular season comes, we will assess the expected crowd and implement it according to the estimated footfall. It will take about a month for the government to develop the portal and everything else, he said, adding that the administration would seek to replicate the existing Char Dham model at Kainchi. How the Char Dham system works The Char Dham registration system the administration is looking to replicate runs through Uttarakhands Tourist Care portal and mobile application. Pilgrims first create an account, then create a tour by entering their travel dates, number of pilgrims, and the Dhams they intend to visit, along with the dates they plan to visit each shrine. They then enter the required details of each pilgrim. Once registration is complete, pilgrims receive a Yatra Registration Letter with a QR code, which they must keep with them. At the destination, designated counters at the shrine verify the registration. The official system describes registration and verification as compulsory for the Char Dham and Hemkund Sahib pilgrimage. Individuals, families, and tour operators can use the system. Pilgrims can register online through the portal or mobile application physical registration facilities and assistance through Yatri Mitra are also available for those unable to complete the process online. The Char Dham system also allows pilgrims to obtain darshan slot tokens, while vehicle registration is part of the system for those travelling by personal or public vehicles. The Kainchi administration now proposes to adapt this broad framework, rather than simply asking pilgrims to provide their names at the temple gate. Behind the decision The proposal follows an unprecedented surge in visitors to the shrine, associated with spiritual leader Neem Karoli Baba. Rayal said the administration normally expects around 25,000 visitors a day at Kainchi Dham. During the long weekend beginning October 2, however, the daily footfall crossed 35,000. The extra visitors overwhelmed the road connecting Kainchi with Bhowali and Mukteshwar. Both the pilgrims and the locals use the same road to Kainchi, which also goes up to Mukteshwar, causing a traffic jam for hours, Rayal said. The congestion stretched through Bhimtal, Bhowali and Kainchi over the long weekend, with vehicles crawling for kilometres and journeys taking hours longer than usual. The administration is now pursuing both crowd management and additional road capacity. A key development discussed at the meeting was the proposed alternative route around Kainchi. Rayal said the Forest Department has now given the required permission for the 18-km Ratighat bypass, which will provide a more direct route towards Almora, Ranikhet and Kausani and help separate through traffic from the road leading to Kainchi. The bypass has received permission from the Forest Department, Rayal said. Earlier, the in-principle approval had been given. Now the practical permission on the ground has also come. Around eight kilometres of the bypass have already been hot-mixed, while work remains on roughly 10 kilometres. Rayal said the state government is currently considering a Rs 21-crore estimate for hot-mixing the remaining stretch. There is a discussion in the government today regarding the Rs 21-crore estimate for hot-mixing it, he said. Once that is approved, the road should become functional in four to six months. According to figures accessed by The Indian Express, 24.34 lakh people visited Kainchi Dham in the first six months of 2026, compared with around eight lakh visitors during the entire previous year. Rayal earlier attributed the latest surge partly to the end of the monsoon, when tourists who had avoided the hills because of rain and landslides began returning, and partly to the release of Hanuman Ansh, a film based on the life and teachings of Neem Karoli Baba.

articleTitle: Shashi Tharoor writes: Boycott is not an election strategy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: opposition boycott
description: Even under imperfect conditions, election campaigns provide a unique platform to raise critical issues, expose executive overreach, and present alternative visions for the country
body_raw: In recent weeks, with the revelations about the Election Commissions troubling conduct and the disenfranchisement of 13 crore voters by unfair means, a provocative debate has emerged. Some are questioning whether opposition parties should continue participating in elections at all, under conditions they claim are fundamentally compromised. Critics point to the systematic erosion of democratic safeguards, the apparent capture of key institutions by mala fide elements, and a playing field tilted heavily in favour of the government. Why should the Opposition, they ask, legitimise a system they believe has been captured by participating in a rigged process? To these critics, continuing to contest elections under the present administration would be an empty ritual that grants a veneer of democratic legitimacy to what they characterise as a managed democracy. They argue for an electoral boycott, saying such a course is rooted in moral clarity by walking away from the ballot box, the Opposition would withhold the democratic stamp of approval that the ruling power relies upon to justify its authority both domestically and internationally. A boycott, from this perspective, is not an act of surrender, but a strategy of non-cooperation designed to expose institutional decay, delegitimise the regime, and shock the public into recognising an existential threat to our democracy. Yet, this logic, however passionately argued, rests on a basic misreading of political power and the nature of state institutions. As the great French diplomat Talleyrand famously observed, les absents ont toujours tort - the missing ones are always wrong. To voluntarily withdraw from the electoral arena is not to delegitimise the governing power it is simply to leave an uncontested field for political opponents to assume untrammelled control over the instruments of the state. In a system where power is derived from constitutional mechanisms, abandoning the battleground means forfeiting every leverage available to protect citizens, influence policy, and hold authority to account. A boycott does not stop the government machinery it merely removes the challenges that an active opposition generates within it. The historical precedent often invoked by proponents of boycotts - Gandhiji and the Indian freedom struggle - illustrates why such a strategy fails in a sovereign republic. Boycotts and civil disobedience were effective tools against British colonial rule because the oppressor was an occupying foreign power. In rejecting a subsidiary role that would have enabled colonial rule, the nationalists demonstrated its complete lack of moral authority. In that context, boycotts were meant to shame the colonial government by exposing the inadequacy of the limited representation it offered. However, a strategy designed against an alien occupier cannot be applied to a sovereign democracy where political actors share a common citizenship and operate under a shared constitutional framework. The Indian National Congress itself recognised this distinction during the Independence movement. While it boycotted elections under the restrictive Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919 to reject a flawed system that enshrined colonial tokenism, it actively chose to participate in the elections under the Government of India Act of 1935, despite limited franchise and communal electorates. Indian leaders recognised that refusing to contest would hand the right of representation to less worthy forces and abandon the public to unmediated colonial authority. In our contemporary constitutional system, choosing non-participation against domestic rivals is not a moral stand, but a spectacular act of self-emasculation. Beyond the misapplication of history, advocating electoral boycott ignores the practical realities of democratic survival. First, political parties are dynamic organisations sustained by public engagement, cadre morale, and local leadership. Abstaining from elections starves a party of its essential lifeblood. Without campaigns to organise around, candidates to field, or local offices to fight for, political cadres will disperse, local networks collapse, and financial resources dry up. Rebuilding an organisational machine after years of non-participation is extraordinarily difficult, if not impossible. A party that retreats from the field of contestation rapidly renders itself irrelevant to the voters it seeks to represent. Second, electoral participation remains the primary mechanism for public mobilisation and civic education. Even under imperfect conditions, election campaigns provide a unique platform to raise critical issues, expose executive overreach, and present alternative visions for the country. When opposition leaders take election campaigns to the streets, hold rallies, and debate policies, they keep democratic discourse alive. Ceding this space entirely to the ruling party guarantees that only one narrative reaches the public, further solidifying the governments grip on popular consciousness and leaving voters who are dissatisfied with the status quo without a voice or a vehicle for change. Furthermore, participating in elections does not mean accepting institutional flaws with blind faith. Rather, it provides the necessary foundation for resisting them. History shows that electoral authoritarians and dominant parties are rarely weakened by moral appeals or voluntary abstentions they are challenged, constrained, and ultimately defeated through persistent, organised resistance at the ballot box. Even in highly uneven contests across the globe, opposition participation has frequently exposed the limits of ruling power, forced unexpected concessions, created internal friction within ruling coalitions, and preserved institutional footholds that later served as launchpads for political renewal. Take Hungary this year Despite facing an illiberal system engineered to entrench Viktor Orbns rule, the Hungarian opposition refused to abandon the ballot box, contesting elections and exposing the regimes failings, ultimately mobilising to deliver a landslide victory. Illiberal autocracies are dismantled through competitive endurance, not voluntary retreat. Democracy is not a fragile artefact that can be preserved by hiding it away from flawed contests it is a muscle that strengthens only through continuous exercise. Complaining about electoral irregularities and demanding institutional accountability are not signs of naive credulity, but the necessary duties of a democratic opposition. To fight in the arena, despite the odds, biases, and structural disadvantages, is the only way for Indian democrats to safeguard the republic. To abstain from contesting would mean handing victory to those who seek to redefine the nations destiny without resistance. We must not abandon the field to them. The writer is a fourth-term Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram

articleTitle: Bihar MLA conviction: When can a legislator be disqualified and seat declared vacant?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: raju singh disqualified
description: Raju Kumar Singh’s conviction has raised questions over his Bihar Assembly seat. Here’s what the law says about disqualification and staying a conviction.
body_raw: The Delhi High Court last week refused to suspend the conviction of Bihar BJP MLA Raju Kumar Singh in a case arising from the death of a woman at a New Years Eve party in Delhi in 2018. Singh was convicted and sentenced to four years imprisonment by Rouse Avenue Court in July. Although the High Court suspended his sentence, it declined to stay the conviction itself. It said, To make things worse, he does not have clean antecedents. There is a long list of cases in which he is found to be involved in. Undoubtedly, in several such cases, he has already been acquitted but it is not a case where he has a clean slate. More than three months after the sentencing, the Bihar Assembly has not declared his seat vacant yet. CPIMLL general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya has questioned the delay, pointing to the assemblys decision to remove his partys MLA Manoj Manzil after his conviction in 2024. The delay raises two questions-does the speaker have any discretion, and can a conviction be put on hold during an appeal? We explain. How can an MLA be disqualified? Article 191 lists the grounds for disqualification from sitting in a state legislature, such as holding an office of profit, being of unsound mind, being an undischarged insolvent, or not being a citizen. Article 1911e disqualifies a person from membership of the state legislature if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament. Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 83 applies to any person who is convicted of any offence and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than two years. It states that such a person shall be disqualified from the date of such conviction and shall continue to be disqualified for six years after release. A conviction is the finding of guilt, and a sentence is a punishment that follows. Singh was sentenced to four years and a month after his conviction was pronounced. Article 190 states several ways a seat is lost, including sitting in both houses of Parliament or two states, staying away from all meetings for sixty days without permission, or resigning, which takes effect only when the Speaker accepts it. Article 1903 a states that if a member is subjected to disqualification, his seat shall thereupon become vacant. Section 151A of the Act requires a by-election within six months from the date of the occurrence of the vacancy, with exceptions. If the seat falls vacant by operation of law, the six months may run from disqualification and not from the notification. Article 193 sets a penalty of five hundred rupees for each day on which a person sits and votes when he knows that he is not qualified or that he is disqualified When does a seat fall vacant? Until 2013, Section 84 of the Act protected a convicted MLA or MP from losing their seat immediately. They could continue in office for three months, and if they filed an appeal within that period, remain a legislator until the appeal was decided. The Supreme Courts 2013 ruling in Lily Thomas v UOI changed that. The court held that Parliament could prescribe the grounds for disqualifying a person but could not postpone the constitutional consequence. Once a member is disqualified, the court said his seat automatically falls vacant under Article 1013a and 1903a. Section 84 was ultra vires the Constitution. The Constitution does provide a route for disputes. Article 1921 provides that if a question arises as to whether a member has incurred a disqualification under Article 1911, the matter goes to the Governor, who acts on the Election Commissions opinion. Neither Article 190 nor 192 names the Speaker. The Speaker decides disqualification only in defection cases under the Tenth Schedule. When a legislator is convictedand the conviction is not disputed, the Commission told the Supreme Court inLok Prahari v ECI 2018 that it does not need to refer the matter to the Governor. It relied on a 1998 Supreme Court ruling in P. V. Narasimha Rao, which concerned MPs. That judgment held that where a disqualification is not disputed, the member ceases to be a member on the date when he incurred the disqualification. The case concerned the MPs, but the scheme for state legislators under Article 192 is materially similar. The Lok Prahari judgment only records this as the commissions submission, not as a holding. In practice, the legislature secretariat issues a notification recording the vacancy. The Lok Sabha Secretariat notified Rahul Gandhis disqualification a day after he was convicted in March 2023. Can convictions be put on hold? Section 430 of the BNSS lets an appellate court suspend the execution of a sentence while an appeal is pending. In Ravi Kant S Patil v Sarvabhouma S Bagali, the Supreme Court held that when a sentence is stayed, the conviction continues to operate. Only a stay of the conviction removes the disqualification. The bench in Lok Prahari said that once conviction is stayed, the disqualification cannot take or remain in effect. When Rahul Gandhi was convicted of criminal defamation in 2023, the Supreme Court said we are of the considered view that the ramifications of sub-section 3 of Section 8 of the Act are wide-ranging. They not only affect the right of the appellant to continue in public life but also affect the right of the electorate, who have elected him, to represent their constituency. It stayed the conviction pending his appeal.

articleTitle: Gurgaon woman spends 50% of salary on rent to live close to work: ‘Saving my peace’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Gurgaon woman rent
description: Shakti Dharni Pandey said she could have chosen a cheaper home farther from her school but decided the time spent commuting was not worth the savings.
body_raw: A Gurgaon woman has explained why she is willing to spend more than half her salary on rent to live just a four-minute walk from her workplace, saying the arrangement gives her something she values more than the money she could save-time, energy, and peace of mind. Shakti Dharni Pandey, who works at a school in Gurgaon, shared her experience in an Instagram video and said she has no intention of moving to a cheaper area, despite knowing many would consider her rent a poor financial choice. More than 50 of my salary goes into my rent, and I am not going to change it. I live in a spacious 1RK that is just a 4-minute walking distance from this school, she said. Living so close to work has allowed Pandey to return home during breaks. And though Im able to come home during class breaks, have a piping hot lunch, and complete my pending work, it costs me way too much. More than half of my school salary goes into rent every single month, which anyone would call a completely bad decision financially, she said. Why she chose a costly home over cheaper rent Pandey said she could have chosen a cheaper home farther from her school but decided the time spent commuting was not worth the savings. I choose this instead of saving money because, from here, I am saving my peace, my energy, and my time, she explained. For Pandey, the benefits go beyond avoiding a daily commute. I dont have to rush in the morning to get ready. I dont have to be in an auto or Metro for long hours to reach home. I also dont have to spend any money on commuting, though it doesnt compensate for the rent, she said. Watch the video View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shakti Dharni Pandey shaktidharni Rather than putting the money in some SIP Pandey described the decision as a way of spending her 20s on herself rather than simply maximising her savings. But the thing is, rather than saving money and putting it in some SIP, I am making my adulting easier, she added. The extra time, she said, gives her room to learn new skills, make videos, and focus on her mental well-being. Pandey also pointed out that her additional income from side projects has helped make the higher rent more manageable. Its not the rent I am paying more than 50 of my salary for it is saving my time, feeling safe and calm, and preserving energy to work on things I want to work on. Thats what I am paying this rent for. And I am not going to change it, she concluded. Pandey shared the video with the caption, Will you do something like this? Pandeys take on rent and convenience prompted a mixed response online. While some Instagram users said they understood her decision, others felt that spending more than half of a salary on housing could create financial difficulties. Just do what makes you happy. Everyone have a different life arc. You go girl, one user wrote. Another said, I can completely relate to it and agree with the perspective that you shared because I Travel almost 2 hours to reach my clg to study. If you are saving money on the commute, food and having enough time. Its worth it, a third user commented. What about those relying on a single income? However, one user pointed out that Pandeys circumstances may make the decision easier to manage than it would be for someone relying on a single income. I think its also important to consider the overall context. Since you have other sources of income, putting 50 of your school salary towards rent may be more manageable for you. For someone who is just starting out with one income source, it might be helpful to first build an emergency fund and some financial stability before allocating such a large portion towards comfort. Just a reminder that everyones financial situation is different, so what works for one person may not work for another, the user wrote.

articleTitle: Kenya reports first Ebola death after traveler from Congo via Uganda dies in Nairobi
articleFeaturedImageAlt: People put on masks at the entrance of The Nairobi Hospital where Kenya's first Ebola virus patient was treated and died, Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Kasuku)
description: Kenya Ebola Case: Kenyan authorities have placed border points on high alert and launched contact-tracing efforts to identify people who may have been exposed to the virus.
body_raw: Kenya Ebola Case Kenya has reported its first confirmed case of Ebola and the countrys first death from the disease, after a man who had been living in Congo for seven years travelled to Nairobi via Uganda, authorities said Tuesday. The man, who had fallen ill about a month ago, was treated at several hospitals before travelling by road to Kampala and later taking a flight to Nairobi. He arrived in the Kenyan capital on Saturday and was admitted to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated and tested positive for Ebola. He died late Monday. Kenyan authorities have placed border points on high alert and launched contact-tracing efforts to identify people who may have been exposed to the virus.

articleTitle: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving ‘mirror image’ mystery
articleFeaturedImageAlt: nobel prize in chemistry
description: The 2026 Nobel Chemistry laureates include Kagan, affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and 95-year-old Soai, who is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science.
body_raw: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2026 on Wednesday in Stockholm to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. The 2026 Nobel Chemistry laureates include Kagan, affiliated with Universit Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and 95-year-old Soai, who is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science. BREAKING NEWS The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the 2026 NobelPrize in Chemistry to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. - The Nobel Prize NobelPrize October 7, 2026 Discovering a new way of manipulating chemical reactions, Kagans findings allowed a greater excess of one of the mirror images to be created than was previously assumed possible. Henri Kagans discovery will be instrumental for chemists who develop reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, flavours, scents and new materials. Thanks to the discoveries that are being recognised by the NobelPrize in Chemistry 2026, chemists have gained fundamental new tools for use in their daily work but, above all, these discoveries have contributed to solving one of chemistrys greatest mysteries how homochirality-like that found in all living beings-can be created. The Soai reaction-developed by 2026 laureate Kenso Soai-has awakened new enthusiasm in chemists who want to understand the lifes origins. Around the world, researchers are now trying to repeat Soais achievement, but with the aim of producing homochiral amino acids and sugars. The non-linear effects that fellow laureate Henri B. Kagan discovered have become an important tool for chemists when they design new reactions. The fact that a reaction is non-linear provides chemists with information about how it occurs. This information can be used to optimise the reaction, so they can obtain the purest possible enantiomers of the product. This is vital for every company that manufactures substances that are intended to interact with living beings, such as pharmaceuticals, flavours, scents and agricultural chemicals. In some cases, it is also important in the production of new materials. - The Nobel Prize NobelPrize October 7, 2026 Meanwhile, Kenso Soai devised the worlds first chemical reaction wherein only one of the potential mirror images was formed. Other than life itself, no one had ever achieved this feat. The Soai reaction is one of the most spectacular chemical experiments ever conducted, the Nobel committee stated. 2026 NobelPrize laureate Henri Kagan discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions, allowing a greater excess of one of the mirror images to be created than was previously assumed possible. His discovery has been revolutionary for chemists who develop reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, flavours, scents and new materials. - The Nobel Prize NobelPrize October 7, 2026 The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three scientists last year for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside. The scientific achievement laid the foundation to potentially suck the greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and harvest moisture from the desert environment, the Associated Press reported. Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry said, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular.

articleTitle: ‘Trust court, go study’: Bombay HC appeals to MPSC protesters, seeks fair exams, recruitment
articleFeaturedImageAlt: MPSC paper leak protest bombay high court
description: The court has asked the Maharashtra government to to ensure "free, impartial and fair" examinations are conducted, as it asked the protesting students to trust the court and 'go study'
body_raw: The Bombay High Court on Wednesday asked the Maharashtra government to address the grievances of the protesting Maharashtra Public Service Commission MPSC aspirants to ensure free, impartial and fair examinations and appealed to the agitators to go back to their studies. It also reminded the MPSC paper leak protesters of state action if they do not relocate, noting that they do not have the required permission. If they protestors wish to continue with the agitation, then they will have to take permission to continue and relocate. If they do not relocate, then the state will have to take reasonable steps, the HC bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna noted. The court was hearing a writ plea by two Pune residents, claiming daily disruptions faced by Pune residents due to agitations by MPSC aspirants at Alka Talkies Chowk, Ahilya Study Centre, and SM Joshi Bridge. Onus is on the state government to ensure recruitment happens and is streamlined, CJ Tripathi orally said, seeking its roadmap within three weeks. It Pune is at a centre for education and most students are genuinely interested in studies and not interested in these protests. The entire atmosphere is now vitiated, and there should be sincere effort in restoring trust.I will make a request to all students, see the plight of parents who have sent you to Pune and go back to education.Innocent children are on roads and their grievances should be addressed and free and fair examination takes place..They should trust the court which is now seized of the matter and do not cause grievance to citizens in peace-loving Pune city, CJ Tripathi orally said. Remarking that students should ask for permission for agitation to ensure citizens are not troubled, the judge added, If they get the idea that there has been something hanky-panky, they have the right to agitate, because they have given hours to study. AG Sathe, appearing for the state government, responded that the governments course of action would be placed on affidavit. We appreciate that. They are students, not anti-socials. Their main grievance is that the examination has to be conducted fairly. The detailed enquiry and everything should be brought on record. We will ensure effort is made and find who the culprits are. Court is genuinely entrusted as guardian and students should go back to faculty and university, the HC remarked and posted further hearing to November 25.

articleTitle: FMGE: NMC says Georgia medical graduates need licence to practise, ‘junior doctor’ status not enough
articleFeaturedImageAlt: fmge exam date
description: The clarification from the NMC came after a candidate filed a grievance on the PM Grievance Portal seeking clarity on the validity of pursuing a six-year MBBS course in Georgia for appearing in the FMGE in India.
body_raw: A foreign medical graduate must hold a licence to practise medicine in the country where they obtained their degree to appear for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination FMGE in India and become eligible for registration as a doctor, rather than merely working as a junior doctor under supervision, as in Georgia. The clarification from the National Medical Commission NMC came after a candidate filed a grievance on the PM Grievance Portal seeking clarity on the validity of pursuing a six-year MBBS course in Georgia for appearing in the FMGE in India. The FMGE is a mandatory requirement for foreign medical graduates seeking registration to practise medicine in India. In its response, the Indian medical regulator, NMC, referred to Regulation 4b of the National Medical Commission Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations, 2021, which imposes an important condition on Indian students who complete their medical education in a foreign country and return to India to take the FMGE. Read Safeguards our healthcare system NMC defends video-based FMGE questions, says they test clinical skills According to the regulation, after completing a medical degree in a foreign country, a candidate must be registered or licensed by the medical regulatory authority of that country to independently practise medicine in a manner equivalent to the licence granted to that countrys own medical graduates. As per Regulation 4b of the FMGL Regulations, 2021, a foreign medical graduate must possess a licence to practise medicine in the country where the medical degree was obtained, at par with the licence granted to citizens of that country, the NMC said in its response to the candidate, Bhawna. Therefore, Junior Doctor status would be sufficient only if it legally permits practice at the required level. If independent medical practice in Georgia is permitted only after completing postgraduate certification then the Junior Doctor status alone would not satisfy Regulation 4b. The matter shall therefore be determined with reference to the applicable law and licensing requirements in Georgia, the NMC added. Also Read NEET PG Counselling 2026 NMC releases institute and course-wise seat matrix Bhawna told that education consultants, allegedly in collusion with several Georgian colleges, are misleading students by incorrectly interpreting the rules regarding medical education in Georgia. These consultants are saying that if you practise as a junior doctor while pursuing or completing your six-year MBBS course called MD in Georgia, you are eligible to appear for the FMGE in India after completing the course. But the NMCs response makes the position clear, she said. Indias Embassy in Yerevan, Armenia - which previously handled Indias diplomatic representation for Georgia as well - issued an advisory in September 2022 to Indian students seeking admission to Georgian medical colleges. The advisory stated that Indian students can work as junior doctors after completing their undergraduate medical studies. However, to practise as independent doctors, they must pass the National Post-Diploma Qualification Examination NPDQE in the Georgian language, pursue postgraduate studies or residency in their chosen speciality, and obtain a licence to practise independently. Since the introduction of the NMCs Regulation 4b, students have faced considerable difficulty in determining which countries provide a licence for independent medical practice after completion of their primary medical qualification, according to medical aspirants and consultants. This has also created scope for confusion, with some consultants and colleges allegedly providing students with interpretations of the rules that may not accurately reflect the applicable licensing requirements. An estimated 30,000 to 40,000 Indian students took admission to several medical colleges in Georgia after the 2021 FMGE regulations came into effect, and many might not be aware that they will not be able to take the FMGE once they return after completing their six-year programme only. They will learn the reality once they are back after the course. The NMC and the Indian Embassy should issue a proper advisory to save the future of thousands of students aspiring to do MBBS from Georgia, a consultant said.

articleFeaturedImageAlt: Akhilesh Yadav Rahul Gandhi Samajwadi Party
description: Sources in Samajwadi Party said the leadership is upset with Congress stealing the show at the INDIA bloc march on Tuesday, but that is not why it skipped the lunch
body_raw: As Opposition MPs gathered at Sagar Ratna in Janpath for a lunch hosted by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Wednesday afternoon, the Samajwadi Party was missing. The absence of Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and other party MPs was conspicuous Yadav and others participated in the INDIA blocs mega march to the Election Commission on Tuesday, and the Kannauj MP was detained and released later. Wednesdays lunch meet, followed by a move towards Jantar Mantar, appeared to be the Oppositions strategy to keep the pressure on the government and further drum up its campaign for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumars resignation over the issues surrounding the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. What Congress said The Congress downplayed the absence of Samajwadi Party MPs. They said most MPs of the Akhilesh Yadav-led party left Delhi last night or this morning and couldnt attend the lunch and protest that followed. In fact, the issue also came up during the lunch where most other INDIA bloc parties were present. Congress general secretary organization KC Venugopal, who coordinated the meeting, told INDIA bloc leaders at Sagar Ratna that the Samajwadi Party MPs left Delhi by the time they were called for the latest protest plan. Amid the buzz, senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh posted a clarification on X, stressing that all alliance parties were invited for lunch. But the decision for the lunch had been taken late last night and communicated. It was therefore natural that some parties could not be represented. There is needless comment in some sections of the media on it. INDIA and other Opposition parties are united and stand in solidarity against Vote Chori, SIR and Delimitation, he said. What SP leaders say Samajwadi Party leaders that The Indian Express spoke to blamed patchy coordination by the Congress. A Samajwadi Party MP said, Samajwadi Party did not attend the lunch of Congress because of lack of proper coordination from the Congress side. Samajwadi Party MPs left for their constituencies on Tuesday evening after the protest against the Chief Election Commissioner ended. By that time, there was no information about the lunch. Had the Congress communicated properly about the lunch programme either to party president Akhilesh Yadav or senior leader Ram Gopal Yadav, MPs from constituencies near Delhi or those still in Delhi would have been asked to participate in the lunch, he said. A Samajwadi Party spokesperson said, I did not receive any invitation call from the Congress or any direction in this regard from Samajwadi Party leadership. The leadership is upset with statements by certain leaders of Congress on the alliance, but that is no reason for skipping the lunch. Samajwadi Party spokesperson Rajendra Chaudhary said Akhilesh Yadav returned to Lucknow Tuesday night. It is possible that the Samajwadi Party received the invitation late. I dont know much about this. But there is no specific reason to skip the lunch today. Sources in Samajwadi Party said the leadership and the MPs are also upset with Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra stealing the show at the INDIA bloc march on Tuesday with the sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan. But that is not the reason for skipping lunch today, said a party MP. It is is true that we are not happy with poor coordination from Congress regarding the protest at Akashvani Bhavan. It was supposed to be a joint protest of the INDIA bloc and not of the Gandhis. The next big election in the country is in Uttar Pradesh where Samajwadi Party has a bigger stake than Congress. Akhilesh Yadav raised the concerns about SIR in Uttar Pradesh more aggressively and effectively while Congress leadership only took symbolic steps during SIR in UP earlier this year. But Congress in Delhi tried to portray that only it was serious about SIR, a party leader said. The Uttar Pradesh subplot The developments surrounding the INDIA bloc offensive against the Election Commission are playing out against a key backdrop the Uttar Pradesh election. In the politically significant heartland state, the Samajwadi Party and the Congress are allies, and as the polls approach, a tussle over seat distribution has begun. The Congress is demanding about 150-200 seats out of the total 403 in Uttar Pradesh, irking Samajwadi Party leaders. Also, the Samajwadi Party has been upset due to public statements by some Congress leaders, including Imran Masood. Masood was last week appointed the UP Congress working president, and the move has reportedly not amused the Samajwadi Party leadership.

articleTitle: Mary Kom’s ex-husband files defamation suit against her amid Bigg Boss stay: ‘It’s a strong case’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mary Kom ex husband
description: Mary Kom's ex-husband Onler has filed a criminal defamation suit against the boxer. She is currently a participant on Bigg Boss 20.
body_raw: Olympic medalist Mary Koms ex-husband Onler Kom is suing the boxer for defamation. As per a report in Hindustan Times, he has initiated criminal defamation proceedings against her under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita BNS. Mary Kom is currently a participant on Bigg Boss 20. Onler has accused Mary Kom of making damaging statements about him on television and via other interviews. Onler confirmed that he was pursuing the matter and told the publication, I have a strong case. I have faith in the judicial system of India. The matter is sub judice, so I wont comment any further. The next hearing is scheduled for November 19. ALSO READ Lost Rs 250 cr in 13 years Rajpal Yadav to SC, hints at film on cheque-bounce cases Mary Koms comments about ex-husband In an earlier appearance on Aap Ki Adalat, Mary Kom had opened up about her relationship with her former husband and accused him of financial misconduct. She claimed that he had cheated her out of crores and had transferred her assets in his name. She also said that he had taken loans in her name. Her comment claiming that her ex-husband did not earn a single penny during their marriage drew a lot of divisive reactions. Soon after, he accused her of having extramarital affairs. Mary Kom later issued a statement in which she said that her comments about Onlers career as a footballer were not meant to disrespect the sport or the people associated with the sport. She insisted that she was overwhelmed during the interview and could not hold back her emotions, and added that she did not mean to insult anyone with her comments The couple got married in 2005, and divorced in 2023 with mutual consent. They share four children. Mary Kom biopic In 2014, a biopic starring Priyanka Chopra was made on Mary Koms life. The film was titled Mary Kom. Darshan Kumar played the role of her husband. Directed by Omung Kumar, the film drew some negative press as many believed that Priyanka Chopra was not the right actor to play the boxer. The film won the Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment at the 62nd National Film Awards.

articleTitle: The Narendra Modi I saw up close
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Prime Minister Narendra Modi
description: That combination of intellectual rigour, decisiveness, accountability and an unwavering focus on outcomes is what, in my view, distinguishes Narendra Modi
body_raw: There are leaders remembered for their soaring political rhetoric, others for electoral victories, and some for the institutions they leave behind. Narendra Modi, in my experience, is best understood through something less obvious His method. Over the years, I had the opportunity to observe him closely, first as an administrator and later from within government. What struck me most was not any single policy decision, but the way he approached problems. Whether the issue was a sweeping national reform or an administrative bottleneck, his first instinct was always diagnosis. He rarely accepted a summary at face value. Instead, the questions would come quickly. What is happening on the ground? Why is it happening? What have you done so far? What exactly is preventing a solution? The questions were not designed to test people. They were designed to test assumptions. Once he understood the reality of a situation, the shift from diagnosis to action was remarkably swift. I saw this most clearly during demonetisation. The decision brought enormous logistical and economic challenges. Long reviews became routine. Every aspect of implementation was being monitored closely. Yet even while dealing with immediate pressures, Modi was already looking beyond the crisis itself. He saw an opportunity to accelerate digital payments across India. He did not view the challenge purely through a technological lens. He understood that ordinary citizens would not embrace digital transactions if commissions and transaction costs remained barriers. Rather than treating those costs as unavoidable, he pursued the issue directly with the Reserve Bank of India. The logic was simple. If friction was preventing adoption, then the friction had to be reduced. Even a vegetable vendor should be able to accept a digital payment. There were, of course, many other questions around currency circulation, cash holdings, gold purchases and the extent to which money returned to the banking system. Yet what I remember most vividly is the relentless focus on solutions. That was characteristic of his approach Identify the obstacle. Understand what sustains it. Remove it. What began as a period of disruption went on to become a major catalyst for Indias digital economy. The same mindset shaped his expectations of those who worked with him. Modi places extraordinary value on preparation. A proposal might appear flawless on paper, but within minutes his questions would reveal whether the presenter truly understood the issue. He expected policymakers to know not only the contents of a brief, but also the larger ecosystem around it The administrative realities, institutional constraints, political implications and impact on citizens. As a result, even routine meetings often became rigorous working sessions. I experienced that standard from the very beginning of my association with him. My first interaction with Modi was brief. Carrying a bouquet, I remarked that I was meeting a Yug Purush, a defining figure of our times. He laughed immediately and brushed aside the compliment, putting me at ease. The more consequential encounter came in May 2014. I was driving home from the NGO I was then running when the late Arun Jaitley called and asked me to report immediately to Gujarat Bhawan. True to form, Modi dispensed with formalities and moved straight to the task at hand. He asked me to examine the political structure of the Union government and recommend which ministries could be merged, streamlined or newly created to improve governance, particularly in the energy, skill and infrastructure sectors, core to Indias future. Working out of a quiet desk in Gujarat Bhawan, I focused on the assignment. Modi was looking for an answer Will this improve governance? That became the lens through which every recommendation was tested. I noticed a fleeting look of disappointment at my presentation. He had expected graphics and presentation, not a stack of paper. It was an early indication of how naturally he gravitated towards technology, visualisation and contemporary tools one could touch, feel, and experience. Shortly afterwards, the Prime Minister conveyed to me that he intended to appoint me as his Principal Secretary. When I raised concerns about restrictions arising from my previous role at TRAI, Jaitley Ji dismissed them with characteristic confidence. Dont bother the Prime Minister with technicalities. The demands of the office became clear almost immediately. Traditionally, the Principal Secretary accompanies the Prime Minister on official foreign visits. I suggested instead that I remain in Delhi, believing I could contribute more by overseeing matters at home while he travelled. His response surprised me. You have lifted a heavy burden off my chest. Modis work ethic recognises neither geography nor time zones. Wherever he travelled, he remained deeply engaged, often calling to review developments, track pending matters and push decisions forward. He was also a keen observer. Ideas encountered abroad, whether in urban infrastructure, public spaces or museum design, often found their way into discussions about governance back home. That same instinct is visible in initiatives such as Yuge Yugeen Bharat. To Modi, a museum is not merely a repository of artefacts. It is a living institution that connects future generations with Indias civilizational journey. Even in matters of culture and heritage, his focus remained on how institutions could educate, engage and endure. Perhaps more than anything else, Modi has little patience for inertia. If an obstacle exists, whether technological, financial or bureaucratic, his instinct is to look for a solution rather than an explanation. That expectation creates pressure, but it also creates clarity. What has earned him the trust of many who work with him, however, is something else his willingness to assume responsibility. During the prolonged opposition against the land acquisition laws, I eventually recommended that the legislation be withdrawn in the larger interest of the agricultural sector. The reforms had arrived ahead of their time and early in his first tenure. He looked at me with a knowing smile. Aap ye keh rahe hain? You are saying this? Yet he agreed. The ordinance lapsed. He is equally quick to acknowledge the contributions of others. Several years before the pandemic, I had suggested distributing surplus grain stocks rather than allowing them to deteriorate in storage. The proposal did not move forward because of fiscal constraints. When Covid-19 struck, however, he immediately saw its relevance. Moments before announcing the programme that would eventually support nearly 80 crore beneficiaries, he was convinced that poverty elimination is a strong argument. Looking back, it is not any single reform, programme or policy decision that best explains Narendra Modi to me. It is a habit of mind. He begins by asking what stands in the way. He refuses to accept cannot as an answer. He presses relentlessly until a solution emerges. Over the years, I have seen that instinct applied to governance, technology, national security, foreign policy, welfare, culture and institution-building alike. The question he returned to repeatedly, whether discussing ministries, digital payments or public policy, was always the same Will this improve governance? That combination of intellectual rigour, decisiveness, accountability and an unwavering focus on outcomes is what, in my view, distinguishes Narendra Modi. It is also why, when I first met him many years ago and referred to him as a Yug Purush, it did not feel like just praise. Time and experience have only reinforced that impression. As a man who continues to redefine our era, Prime Minister Modis mark will remain indelible in the annals of history. The writer is Chairperson, Prime Ministers Museum and Library, Chairman, Temple Construction Committee, Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust. He served as Principal Secretary to Prime Minister Narendra Modi during 2014-2019

articleTitle: Ahead of CJP’s October 10 protest, Delhi Police puts 2,800 ‘criminals’ on radar
articleFeaturedImageAlt: According to sources in the Delhi Police, all those with criminal antecedents who were spotted by the Facial Recognition System (FRS) during the July protests will be tracked by their local police stations. (Express Photo)
description: 2,873 people who took part in the CJP’s July Jantar Mantar protests were flagged for criminal records, with police now working to stop them from reaching Delhi ahead of October 10.
body_raw: The Delhi Police had identified 2,800-odd people with a criminal background who took part in the Cockroach Janta Partys July protests against the NEET paper leak at Jantar Mantar. Efforts are on to ensure none of them reach Delhi on October 10, senior officials told The Indian Express. The CJP has announced that the Jantar Mantar 2.0 protest, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner CEC Gyanesh Kumar, will start on October 10. According to sources in the Delhi Police, all those with criminal antecedents who were spotted by the Facial Recognition System FRS during the July protests will be tracked by their local police stations. Permission to protest has not been granted yet. So police stations will track if people with a history of serious offences, especially the ones who came last time, are heading towards the protest site. The idea is to not let them come here and disrupt law and order in the area, said a police officer on condition of anonymity. At least 2,873 people with criminal records had been flagged by the FRS 989 of them were accused in heinous cases, 101 named in murder cases, and at least 42 were involved in two or more murders. The Indian Express reported that at least 25 of them, accused of serious crimes such as murder, attempted murder, rape and child abuse, were even supposed to be in jail. Students told to keep away Apart from tracking criminals, police are also looking to inform students that any assembly on October 10 in the New Delhi area would be unlawful, said a senior police officer. Public meetings with members of Residents Welfare Associations RWAs in areas with dense student populations are usually a regular feature. Now, a senior officer said, PG owners are specifically being made aware of the law and order situation in the capital in these meetings. We are asking PG owners to inform students that Section 163 of the BNSS is in force in the New Delhi district. So any protest in the area is illegal and students should be considerate of that, said a senior cop. Focus on city borders The border areas are also a focus for the Delhi Police. Another senior officer told The Indian Express that police will be on a lookout for large groups of people who are looking to enter Delhi before Saturday. The main focus areas will be the Uttar Pradesh border, which touches East Delhi and Shahdara, Haryana border, which touches Dwaraka, and the Rajasthan border, which touches Southwest Delhi. Any mass movement will be tracked through borders. We will be putting up barricades for checks on routes going towards New Delhi, so that large groups of people dont assemble, said a senior police officer. Earlier in the day, Saurab Das, co-convener of the CJP, reached Parliament Street police station to submit a letter saying they have the right to protest at the designated site at Jantar Mantar. Das, along with All India Students Association AISA president Neha Bora, held a press conference at the Press Club of India in the afternoon where they announced a joint call to citizens to gather at Jantar Mantar to save the democracy of the country. Speaking to the media, Das said he did not seek permission from the Delhi Police but informed them that they would hold a protest against the Special Intensive Revision SIR and CEC Kumar.

articleTitle: Even if Gyanesh Kumar resigns, we won’t stop: CJP, students on Jantar Mantar protest
articleFeaturedImageAlt: AISA National President Neha Bora addresses a joint press conference at the Press Club of India, New Delhi on Wednesday. CJP Chief spokesperson Sourav Das, SFI and ASAP representatives also present. (ANI Photo)
description: Saurav Das, CJP co-convener, reached the Parliament Street police station in the morning to submit the letter to the DCP's office.
body_raw: Announcing a joint protest at Delhis Jantar Mantar on October 10 against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the Cockroach Janta Party CJP and several student organisations on Wednesday submitted a formal intimation letter to the Delhi Police informing them about the proposed agitation. Saurav Das, CJP co-convener, reached the Parliament Street police station in the morning to submit the letter to the DCPs office. Asked whether they sought permission for the protest, Das said, Please dont use the word permission. Who is Delhi Police to give us permission? Maintaining that intimation is sufficient, he added that they provided undertakings to the police. We will cooperate with Delhi Police and we hope Delhi Police will cooperate with us, he said. After handing over the letter, Das, along with All India Students Association AISA president Neha Bora and others, held a press conference at the Press Club of India. The press conference brought together CJP, AISA, All India Students Federation AISF and Students Federation of India SFI. The Aam Aadmi Partys student wing, Association of Students for Alternative Politics ASAP, also participated. Das urged people across the country to travel to Delhi and to come prepared for a prolonged agitation. This fight is not going to be easy. I appeal to everyone across the country to join us, book train and flight tickets, he said. Even if Kumar resigns, the protesters will not step back because the electoral system needs to be cleaned up, he added. We not only demand the removal of Gyanesh Kumar but also the appointment of a new CEC in a democratic manner. It is high time that democratic reforms are carried out in the electoral roll system so that no other Gyanesh Kumar can commit vote chori in the future. He also demanded that a criminal case be registered against Kumar for allegedly carrying out irregularities in the electoral roll process. Das alleged that they had received information that Delhi Police personnel were harassing female protesters and that right-wing groups were being mobilised to disrupt the October 10 protest. Citing a September 23 report in The Indian Express, Bora said, Whatever our suspicions regarding the electoral rolls were found to be correct. The report had revealed that two of the three Election Commissioners - Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi - had recorded at least 14 objections over 10 months, including controversial changes made to Form 6 and handling of voter deletions during the Special Intensive Revision SIR process, among others. Since then, we have been seeing protests on the streets demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar. The call given by people like Yogendra Yadav, Manoj Jha, Prashant Bhushan and Anjali Bhardwaj proved that, in the coming days, the fight needs to be carried out in a consolidated and united manner. That is how we fought and showed our unity during the July education-related movement, she added. The October 2 protest called by AISA in Delhi and CJP in Mumbai witnessed a huge participation of people, she said. This shows that vote theft is the biggest issue in this country right now. Backing the INDIA bloc MPs who tried to march towards the EC office on Tuesday demanding Kumars resignation, Bora said elected representatives have a duty to take to the streets to raise peoples issues and defend their rights. Thats what the MPs of the INDIA bloc did, she said. Meanwhile, Delhi Police officers said the protest would not be allowed as prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita were in force across Parliament Street and adjoining areas. In July, a CJP-led agitation over the NEET paper leak had forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign as Union Education minister.

articleTitle: How RBI’s rate hike turns homeownership dream into bigger debt burden
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra and MPC members at a press conference on its Monetary Policy announcement and repo rate hike from 5.25% to 5.50%, (RBI/ANI Video Grab)
description: When RBI raises the price of money, borrowers pay — through higher EMIs, longer loan tenures, bigger down payments, and delayed dreams of home ownership. How is that? We explain.
body_raw: A 25-basis-point bps repo rate hike may seem insignificant on paper, but for a homebuyer, it is anything but small. On a Rs 50 lakh home loan taken for 20 years, a 25-bps increase can mean roughly Rs 780 more in monthly equated monthly installment EMI, and nearly Rs 1.88 lakh in additional interest outgo over the life of the loan, experts say. For a household already struggling to make the down payment and qualify for a loan, the Reserve Bank of Indias RBIs rate decision can turn an affordable home into an unaffordable liability. Loans linked to the marginal cost of funds-based lending rate MCLR may also become more expensive. Banks, however, have flexibility in revising MCLR-based rates depending on their funding costs, liquidity conditions and deposit mobilisation. Heres how a repo rate hike feeds into home-loan costs - and why first-time buyers often feel the impact the most. How repo rate affects borrowing costs The pain does not stop with the EMI. The RBIs repo rate is the price at which banks borrow from the central bank. When that rate rises, borrowing costs across the financial system tend to move up. Floating-rate home-loan borrowers are particularly exposed because their interest rates are linked, directly or indirectly, to benchmark rates-the repo rate. The increase can either push up the EMI or force the borrower to stay indebted for longer. According to experts, banks may choose to increase the loan tenure rather than allow the EMI to jump sharply. That may soften the immediate monthly shock, but it is hardly a free lunch. A longer tenure means the borrower remains in debt for more years and can end up paying considerably more interest. Why first-time buyers bear more For first-time homebuyers, the problem is even more severe. Loan eligibility is determined partly by the borrowers income and repayment capacity. Higher interest rates reduce the amount a household can borrow for the same EMI. The buyer is then forced to either settle for a cheaper property, arrange a larger down payment or postpone the purchase. In the countrys already expensive urban housing markets, that is a serious blow. Many real estate companies are saddled with unsold stocks in cities such as Mumbai. The blunt reality is this when the RBI raises the price of money, borrowers pay - through higher EMIs, longer loan tenures, bigger down payments, and delayed dreams of home ownership. For the countrys aspiring middle class, that is not a statistical footnote, but a direct hit to affordability. RBIs rate hike after over 3 years a shift in policy Along with the hike in its key policy rate, which is the first rate hike since February 2023, the central bank has also signaled a shift towards tighter monetary policy amid rising inflationary pressures, elevated crude oil prices and a challenging global interest-rate environment. The Monetary Policy Committee MPC has changed the policy stance to calibrated tightening from neutral indicating further hike in the interest rates is a likelihood. The policy panel has also hiked the growth projection from 6.7 to 7.1 in FY27 in the wake of the higher economic activity in the country. The panel also raised the inflation forecast to 5.2 for FY27 from 5 previously. The six-member MPC headed by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has sent a hawkish message the era of easy money is almost over, and borrowers should brace themselves for more pain. The MPCs decision to shift its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening is not a mere change in terminology - it is a clear warning that the central bank is prepared to tighten the screws if inflationary pressures refuse to ease.

articleTitle: New role for actor Mithun Chakraborty in Bengal government, with cabinet rank
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mithun Chakraborty
description: The administrative circles believe that the scope of his responsibilities and his specific role as an advisor would become clear in the next steps.
body_raw: The West Bengal government on Wednesday appointed veteran actor and BJP leader Mithun Chakraborty as a cultural advisor with the rank of a Cabinet Minister. He has been appointed as an advisor in the Information and Culture Department with immediate effect, as per a recent notification issued by the Personnel and Administrative Reforms Department. The notification stated, The Governor is pleased to appoint Shri Mithun Chakraborty as Advisor to the Government of West Bengal in the rank of Cabinet Minister in the Information and Cultural Affairs Department, with an immediate effect and until further order. The administrative circles believe that the scope of his responsibilities and his specific role as an advisor would become clear in the next steps. According to sources in Nabanna, Mithun will take charge of the new post very soon. At present, the veteran actor is in Alipurduar for a shooting assignment. From there, Mithun has thanked Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari for entrusting him with this new responsibility. Recently, at the stage of the foundation-laying ceremony for the Uttam Kumar Film Centre in New Town, the Chief Minister had announced that Mithun Chakraborty would be appointed as the state governments cultural advisor, owing to his contributions to the film industry as well as his connection with West Bengal. The Suvendu Adhikari-led state government had also sought his advice during the centenary celebrations of Uttam Kumar, apart from several areas such as tourism. The veteran actor had joined the BJP in 2021. He also had a brief stint with the Trinamool Congress when Mamata Banerjee had nominated him for Rajya Sabha in 2014. However, he resigned from the Upper House in 2016. The veteran actor had joined the BJP in 2021. In a stellar career spanning five decades, Mithun has acted in and produced several films, earning the moniker Mahaguru The Great Teacher in the Bengali cinema world.

articleTitle: India calls for de-escalation after Black Sea ship attacks
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Black Sea attacks on Indian seafarers
description: “A Togo-flagged ship, Alfa Watan, was attacked yesterday and the fate of its crew is unknown,” said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal.
body_raw: After four commercial ships with Indian seafarers were attacked in the Black Sea in less than 36 hours, India on Wednesday once again called for dialogue and diplomacy to de-escalate tensions and enable the early return of peace to the region. The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest, the Ministry of External MEA official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Wednesday. We have seen a string of attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea region. We condemn such attacks that threaten commercial shipping and endanger the lives of our seafaring community, he said. Listing out the four incidents, he said that the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov came under attack while it was plying in the Black Sea. There were three Indian nationals onboard. One of them was injured and has since received medical treatment, he said, adding that the Indian embassy in Romania is in touch with them for their safety and welfare. We thank the Romanian authorities for their support and swift action, he said. A Togo-flagged ship, Alfa Watan, was attacked yesterday and the fate of its crew is unknown, he said. Another vessel, Palau-flagged MV ABLE, came under a drone attack, but fortunately all its 18 crew, including 7 Indian nationals, have been rescued. One Indian national suffered injuries and is under medical supervision, the MEA spokesperson said, and thanked the Bulgarian authorities for their timely help. Our Mission in Bulgaria is offering all possible assistance to our seafarers, he said. The fourth ship which came under attack is the Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio, an oil tanker. All the crew, consisting of 23 Indian seafarers, have been rescued, he said. The Liberia-flagged vessel carrying oil, with a crew of 23 Indian nationals, came under attack by drone boats off Russias Black Sea coast, Russian authorities said. The crew has been saved and evacuated to shore, a spokesman for the Russian transport ministry told state-run TASS news agency. The Aframax Rio tanker came under attack on Tuesday by unmanned surface vessels USVs, and open fire is raging in the Black Sea waters, the Russian transport ministry said. The ministry said the vessels all Indian crew of 23 was saved and none was hurt. The incident took place near Sochi, Russias popular resort city on the Black Sea coast. When asked about the Indian proposal to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the MEA spokesperson said, On the issue of the Ukraine conflict, India has consistently maintained that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward. On Sunday, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said India has moved beyond advocacy and stepped up its efforts in recent months to resolve the Ukraine conflict by engaging in conversations with both Kyiv and Moscow. In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that India has declared its readiness to make a feasible contribution to resolving the Ukraine conflict and Russia is grateful to New Delhi for such willingness. Indeed, India is declaring readiness to make a feasible contribution to resolving the situation surrounding Ukraine, Peskov was quoted as saying by the state-run TASS news agency. His statement came days after Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described Indias proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the broadest among four offers received by Kyiv. The other proposals had come from Turkiye, Egypt and the US. We have four proposals. The broadest one is Indias proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in this combination, Sybiha had told reporters in Kyiv last week.

articleTitle: ‘3 ICC trophies, 2 Asia Cups, back-to-back Asian Games gold’: BCCI lauds outgoing selector Agarkar
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Ajit Agarkar
description: BCCI lauded outgoing chairman of selectors Ajit Agarkar for three ICC trophies, two Asia Cups and back-to-back Asian Games gold.
body_raw: The Board of Control for Cricket in India BCCI has lauded outgoing chairman of selectors Ajit Agarkar for his commitment, conviction and contribution over the last three years, as his tenure officially came to an end. Agarkars term concluded last month, and the BCCI on Tuesday invited applications to fill the vacant post, following weeks of speculation over whether he would be considered for an extension. A tenure marked by some truly special moments for Indian cricket - three ICC trophies, two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games Gold medals, along with a run to the 2023 ODI World Cup final, the BCCI posted on its official X account. Thank you, Mr Ajit Agarkar for your commitment, conviction and contribution as Chairman of the Mens Selection Committee. Wishing you the very best for the journey ahead, the apex cricket governing body added. A tenure marked by some truly special moments for Indian cricket - three ICC trophies, two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games Gold medals, along with a run to the 2023 ODI World Cup final. Thank you, Mr Ajit Agarkar imAagarkar, for your commitment, conviction and contribution as Chairman of the Mens Selection Committee. Wishing you the very best for the journey ahead. - BCCI BCCI October 7, 2026 India won the 2024 and 2026 T20 World Cups, along with the 2025 Champions Trophy, during Agarkars tenure. He also oversaw a significant transition that involved the T20 and Test retirements of batting greats Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma. History would be kinder The BCCIs message followed head coach Gautam Gambhirs note of thanks to Agarkar earlier in the day. Gambhir said history would be kinder to Agarkar, whose conviction in the team first theory was crucial to India winning three ICC trophies during his tenure. Dear Ajit Bhai, an absolute honour to work with you. Those 3 ICC trophies are a testimony of your conviction Team first Team ahead, always. I must say, History will be kinder to you. Thank you for everything. My heartfelt wishes for your future endeavours Gambhir wrote on X. Former India cricketer R Ashwin also spoke in Agarkars defence on his YouTube channel, acknowledging the difficulty of the decisions the selector had to make. The fact is that Ajit Agarkar had the responsibility to take a lot of big decisions in this stint he had to phase out the senior players, and it cannot be easy. I was one of the senior players phased out during his tenure, but still by keeping some distance from that, I want to say that he has been a very good chairman of selectors, Ashwin said. Agarkars tenure was a mixed one in the eyes of many. He delivered silverware but also drew heavy criticism for some of the tough calls he made after taking charge in July 2023. According to sources, Agarkar did not seek an extension, which led the BCCI to look for a new chief selector. This paper had reported in August that BCCI officials were set to meet Agarkar to discuss a one-year extension after Indias tour of Sri Lanka, amid differences over Rohit Sharmas ODI future in the lead-up to the 2027 ODI World Cup.
